questions.q: Why does this lesson say sandbox access shouldn't automatically mirror whatever a user has in production?
options: Because Salesforce technically prevents sandbox and production access from ever matching
Because only system administrators are ever granted sandbox access

Because some users need broader sandbox access than production would suggest (like a contractor building in a Developer sandbox), and others need narrower access (like a sales rep who has no reason to access a Full sandbox's real data)
Because sandbox access is always identical to production access by Salesforce design, with no exceptions possible
questions.explain: Access needs can run in either direction relative to production -- broader for someone who needs to build without touching production, narrower for someone with no legitimate reason to see the same real data in a less-controlled sandbox.

questions.q: What specific control does this lesson describe for limiting who can log into a sandbox?
options: Scoping sandbox access to a specific, defined group of users rather than leaving it open to every active user by default
Disabling all login access to every sandbox permanently
Requiring a password reset every time someone logs into a sandbox
Deleting the sandbox immediately after creation
questions.explain: Scoping access to a defined group directly shrinks exposure -- a Full sandbox with real data is far less risky once only the people who actually need it for a specific project can log in.

questions.q: What does "least privilege" mean in the environment-access context this lesson describes?
options: Granting the maximum access possible to avoid future requests
Granting access scoped to what a specific, current need actually requires, not copied automatically from a different environment or granted broadly just in case
A rule that applies only to production, never to sandboxes
Granting access only to users who have worked at the company for over five years
questions.explain: Least privilege, applied to environments, means access should be justified by an actual current need in that specific environment -- not inherited wholesale from a user's production access.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say access review needs to apply to sandboxes, not just production?
options: Because sandboxes automatically revoke access after 30 days with no review needed
Because Salesforce legally requires quarterly sandbox reviews for all orgs

Because a sandbox access list that's never reviewed only ever grows, and organizations often apply this discipline to production while neglecting it for sandboxes entirely -- exactly how the contractor scenario from Lesson 9 happens
Because sandbox access reviews are only needed for Developer sandboxes, not Full or Partial Copy
questions.explain: The same review questions (is this access still needed, has a time-boxed need's window closed) apply to sandboxes just as much as production -- and are more often skipped there, which is exactly how stale access accumulates.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a mature environment strategy apply BOTH data masking (Lesson 10) and scoped access control, rather than relying on just one?
options: Because masking and access control are actually the same control with two different names
Because Salesforce requires both controls to be configured before a sandbox can be created at all
Because access control alone is always sufficient, making masking unnecessary
Because defense that depends on only one control is more fragile than defense that layers two -- masking shrinks the data side of the risk, while access scoping shrinks who can reach it
questions.explain: This lesson explicitly frames masking and access scoping as addressing two different sides of the same risk -- the data itself, and who can reach it -- and recommends layering both rather than relying on either alone.
